# Introduction \label{Introduction}

Note: I was not sure what the desired output for this was so I just went with a Texevier pdf :)

This report will construct a Global Balanced Index Fund using a mix of traded global and local indexes. A balanced fund holds a mix of asset classes, such as equities, bonds and commodities, and typically follows a strategic asset allocation that is re-evaluated over time. As the fund is built from indexes, the main decision is how much to allocate to each index. The fund is rebalanced every quarter and must meet a set of limits on its exposures, which are set out in Section \ref{Construction}.

# Data and approach \label{Data}

This section will look at the assets that the fund can hold:

* Global equity: MSCI USA, Europe, Japan and Emerging Markets indexes.
* Local equity: the J200, the Mid Cap index (J201), the value and momentum style indexes and listed property (J253).
* Bonds: the ALBI and inflation-linked bonds (CILI) locally, and US, German and UK 10 year government bonds globally.
* Commodities: gold and the Bloomberg Commodity Index.

The bond data is given as yields, so these were first converted to monthly returns (as per the instructions in the exam paper). The return is calculated as last month’s yield divided by twelve, minus the modified duration multiplied by the change in yield. Modified duration refers to how sensitive a bond’s price is to a change in its yield and 9 was used based on the average yield since 2010 (see root readme). Therefore, the bond returns are an approximation.

```{r Rets_Universe}
# Asset class and region of each asset (used for the group limits)
ref <- bind_rows(tibble(Name = c("MSCI_USA", "MSCI_EU", "MSCI_Jap", "MSCI_EM"),
         Class = "Equity", Region = "Global"),
  tibble(Name = c("J200", "J201", "STXVALJ433", "STXMOMJ433", "J253"),
         Class = "Equity", Region = "Local"),
  tibble(Name = c("US_10Yr", "Germany_10Yr", "UK_10Yr"),
         Class = "Bonds", Region = "Global"),
  tibble(Name = c("ALBITR", "CILITR"),
         Class = "Bonds", Region = "Local"),
  tibble(Name = c("Gold", "Bcom_Index"),
         Class = "Commodities", Region = "Global"))

# Monthly returns of all assets in one data frame
Q4_Returns <- Q4_Build_Fund(MSCI, Bond_Yields, Commods, Idx_Daily, LCL_Yield, ref)
```

```{r Table_Assets, results = 'asis'}
# Class, region, first month and number of months of each asset
Asset_Tab <-
  Q4_Returns %>%
  group_by(Name, Class, Region) %>%
  summarise(Start = format(min(date), "%b %Y"), Months = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(Class, Region)

Table <- xtable(Asset_Tab, caption = "Assets available to the fund \\label{Table_Assets}")
print(Table, type = "latex", comment = FALSE, include.rownames = FALSE, table.placement = 'H')
```

# Constructing the fund \label{Construction}

This section will look at how the weights of the fund are chosen. The fund must meet the following requirements:

* Long-only strategy.
* When using covariance and mean forecasts, use a look-back of at least 10 years.
* Do not hold any assets with less than 5 years' returns data.
* Apply quarterly rebalancing.
* Limit exposure to bonds and credit instruments at 25%.
* Limit exposure to equities at 75%.
* Limit exposure to commodities to 15%.
* Limit single asset exposure to 35%.
* Global exposure limit 60%.

The fund is also fully invested, tbus the weights sum to one.

With these limits kept in mind, the weights are chosen so that the fund has the lowest possible variance. Minimum variance is an objective optimisation technique, as it does not depend on a risk or return preference. The accuracy of an optimiser out of sample depends on the quality of the return forecasts and the stability of the covariance matrix. Therefore, minimum variance was chosen as it does not need return forecasts. It only uses the covariance matrix, and this shows how the assets move together. Outliers have a large effect on the covariance matrix. For this reason, it is estimated using Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage. Shrinkage pulls the most extreme coefficients toward more central values and reduces estimation error. The covariance matrix also needs a full square matrix of returns with no missing values. Some assets only have between five and ten years of data and therefore have gaps in the ten year window. These gaps are filled with random draws from each asset’s own return distribution. This preserves the distribution of each asset.

```{r Roll_Weights, cache = TRUE}
# wide return matrix from 2010 onwards
return_mat <-
  Q4_Returns %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20100101)) %>%
  select(date, Name, Returns) %>%
  spread(Name, Returns)

# quarter-end rebalance dates
EOM_datevec <-
  return_mat %>% select(date) %>% unique %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == last(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(format(date, format = "%m"))) %>% filter(Months %in% c(3, 6, 9, 12)) %>%
  pull(date) %>% unique

# minimum variance weights at each rebalance date
Q4_Weights <-
  EOM_datevec %>% map_df(~Q4_Roll_Optimizer(return_mat, EOM_datevec = ., ref, LookBackSel = 120))
```


# Results \label{Results}

This section will look at how the fund performed compared to two other portfolios. The first is a strategic balanced allocation, which holds fixed weights based on the published benchmark weights of a South African balanced index fund [@satrix2026] (see Satrix Balanced Index fund pdf in the bin folder). These are 40% in the Capped SWIX, 30% in MSCI World, 8% in MSCI Emerging Markets, 17% in the ALBI, 3% in listed property and 2% in cash (STeFI). Its weights are reset on the same quarterly dates as the fund. The second is the Capped SWIX on its own, which shows how the fund compares to holding only local equities.

```{r Port_Returns}
# minimum variance fund returns
MinVol_Rets <- Q4_Port_Returns(Weights = Q4_Weights %>% select(date, Tickers, Weight = minvol), Returns = Q4_Returns %>% select(date, Tickers = Name, Returns), Name = "Minimum variance")

# monthly returns for the strategic balanced allocation
ref_bm <- tibble(Name = c("J433", "MSCI_AllWorld", "MSCI_EM", "ALBITR", "J253", "STEFI"))
BM_Returns <- Q4_Build_Fund(MSCI, Bond_Yields, Commods,
                            bind_rows(Idx_Daily, STeFI %>% select(date, Tickers, Returns)),
                            LCL_Yield, ref_bm)

# Create the benchmark with fixed weights, reset on the same quarter-end dates as the fund
Port_BM <- tibble(Tickers = c("J433", "MSCI_AllWorld", "MSCI_EM", "ALBITR", "J253", "STEFI"),
                  Weight  = c(0.40, 0.30, 0.08, 0.17, 0.03, 0.02))

BM_Weights <- unique(Q4_Weights$date) %>% map_df(~Port_BM %>% mutate(date = .x))

BM_Rets <- Q4_Port_Returns(Weights = BM_Weights,
                           Returns = BM_Returns %>% select(date, Tickers = Name, Returns),
                           Name = "Strategic balanced allocation")

# equity-only comparison: Capped SWIX over the same months
SWIX_Rets <-
  BM_Returns %>%
  filter(Name == "J433", date > min(Q4_Weights$date)) %>%
  select(date, Returns) %>%
  mutate(Tickers = "Capped SWIX")
```

```{r Figure_Cum, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Cumulative returns \\label{Figure_Cum}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# All three return series in one data frame
All_Rets <- bind_rows(MinVol_Rets, BM_Rets, SWIX_Rets)

g_cum <-
  All_Rets %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  # start every series at 1
  mutate(CP = CP / first(CP)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, CP, color = Tickers)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Returns",
       subtitle = "Minimum variance fund vs strategic balanced allocation and Capped SWIX",
       x = "Year", y = "Growth of R1 invested in 2020",
       caption = "Note:\nAll portfolios start in January 2020.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = T)

fmxdat::finplot(g_cum)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_Cum} shows the growth of R1 invested in the fund and the two comparison portfolios since January 2020. As all three portfolios start on the same date, the comparison is not distorted by different start dates. The fund fell by less than both comparison portfolios during the 2020 market decline (Covid period). However, it grew more slowly from 2022 onwards and ends up below both the strategic balanced allocation and the Capped SWIX at the end of the period. This suggests that the fund offers more protection when markets fall, but that clearly comes with the cost of gains when the market experiences an upswing.

```{r Figure_DD, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Drawdowns \\label{Figure_DD}", fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
# drawdown is the fall from the highest cumulative value reached so far
g_dd <-
  All_Rets %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Drawdown, color = Tickers)) +
  labs(title = "Drawdowns: Minimum Variance Fund and Comparison Portfolios", subtitle = "Fall from the previous peak", x = "Year", y = "Drawdown") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_DD} shows the drawdowns of each portfolio, which measure how far a portfolio falls from its previous peak. The fund had the smallest drawdown in 2020 and near the end of the sample. In 2022, however, its drawdown was similar to that of the strategic balanced allocation. Therefore, the lower volatility of the fund did not always lead to smaller losses.

```{r Figure_Weights, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Weights plot \\label{Figure_Weights}", fig.height = 5, fig.width = 7, fig.ext = 'png'}
g_wts <-
  Q4_Weights %>%
  # order the assets by class so each class is stacked together
  mutate(Tickers = factor(Tickers, levels = ref$Name)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(date, minvol, fill = Tickers), stat = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Weights Plot", subtitle = "Stacked bar of the fund weights at each quarterly rebalance", x = "Year", y = "Weight") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_wts, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Figure \ref{Figure_Weights} shows the weights of the fund at each rebalance. The limits on bonds, commodities and global assets are binding at every rebalance, so the split between asset classes stays the same throughout. The optimiser therefore mainly decides which assets to hold within each class. Gold makes up most of the commodity weight for most of the period. The local equity indices only enter the fund once they have five years of data and MSCI Japan has the largest global equity weight (over the period). As the global returns are in USD and the local returns in ZAR, part of the preference for global assets may be due to currency movements. Therefore, the weights should be interpreted with caution.

```{r Table_Stats, results = 'asis'}
# Statistics relative to the strategic balanced allocation, over the last 3 and 5 years
Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(All_Rets %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret = Returns), BM = "Strategic balanced allocation", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(All_Rets %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret = Returns), BM = "Strategic balanced allocation", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  ) %>%
  mutate(Period = as.character(Period))

Table <- xtable(Tab_stats, caption = "Fund Moments Comparison: relative to the strategic balanced allocation \\label{Table_Stats}", digits = 3)
```

Table \ref{Table_Stats} compares the three portfolios over the last three and five years, with the strategic balanced allocation as the benchmark. The fund has the lowest volatility over both periods, as well as the smallest average drawdown and the smallest modified CVaR. Its beta is also below one, which means that it moves less than the benchmark. However, this lower risk came with lower returns (as we saw in the cummulative returns figure). Over five years, the fund’s annualised return is below that of the benchmark and its information ratio is negative over both periods. Over the last three years, the fund earned a similar return to the Capped SWIX with much lower volatility. This suggests that the fund achieves what a minimum variance approach aims for (lower risk), but it did so at the cost of some of the returns.

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

This report constructed a Global Balanced Index Fund that minimises variance within the given limits and is rebalanced every quarter. The limits on bonds, commodities and global assets were binding throughout. Thus, the split between asset classes was largely set by the limits and the optimiser mainly chose the assets within each class. The fund had lower volatility than both the strategic balanced allocation and the Capped SWIX and it declined by less during sharp equity declines. However, it also earned lower returns and its losses were not always smaller than those of the benchmark. These results should be interpreted with caution, due to the short sample and the global returns are in USD and the bond returns are approximations. As the output of an optimiser is a guide rather than the truth, the weights are best used as a starting point for further discussion.
